stem.text: Let f be a continuous function with \( f(1) = -1 \), \( f(3) = 4 \). Let \( g(x) = \int_{2 x + 1}^{0} f(t) \, dt \). Find the value of \( g'\left(1\right) \).

worked_solution.text: Reversing the limits, \( g(x) = -\int_{0}^{2 x + 1} f(t) \, dt \), so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus its derivative is minus the integrand evaluated at \( 2 x + 1 \).
The chain rule multiplies by the derivative of \( 2 x + 1 \), which is \( 2 \).
At \( x = 1 \) the limit is \( 3 \) and its derivative is \( 2 \).

parameter_draw.form: composite limit in the lower position

difficulty_variables.upper limit equal to x versus a function: composite limit in the lower position

distractor_derivations.A: -f(3) with the factor u'(1) = 2 left off
distractor_derivations.C: integrand evaluated at x = 1 instead of at the limit 3
distractor_derivations.D: sign of the reversed limits lost, as if the variable limit were the upper limit
